items.stem: You join orders to customers but want every order kept even when no matching customer row exists. Which join do you use?

options.text: LEFT JOIN with orders on the left
options.rationale: Correct: a LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table regardless of matches.
An INNER JOIN drops rows that have no match.
A CROSS JOIN produces every combination, not matched rows.
A self join relates a table to itself; it does not preserve unmatched rows by itself.

items.explanation: Correct: a LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table regardless of matches.

items.stem: Which clause filters rows after aggregation, for example to keep only groups with SUM over a threshold?

options.rationale: Correct: HAVING filters grouped results after aggregation.
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping.
LIMIT caps the number of returned rows, it does not filter by aggregate.
ORDER BY sorts; it does not filter.

items.explanation: Correct: HAVING filters grouped results after aggregation.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about PostgreSQL indexes are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: A B-tree index can speed up equality and range lookups on a column
options.rationale: Correct: B-tree indexes support equality and ordered range scans.

options.text: Indexes add overhead to inserts and updates
options.rationale: Correct: each index must be maintained on write, adding cost.

options.text: Adding more indexes always improves overall performance
options.rationale: Excess indexes slow writes and may never be used.

options.text: An index guarantees a query will never do a sequential scan
options.rationale: The planner may still choose a sequential scan when it is cheaper.

items.explanation: Correct: B-tree indexes support equality and ordered range scans.; Correct: each index must be maintained on write, adding cost.
